newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - US T-bond volatilities little changed.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - US T-bond volatilities little changed.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. Treasury bond options were little changed in dull, typical Monday trade as the market awaited Friday's February U.S. employment report, dealers said.
The second part of Fed Chairman Greenspan's semi-annual Humphrey Hawkins testimony on Wednesday also kept the market cautious and subdued activity, they added.
Implied volatilities for April and June T-bond futures options were a touch off early highs but virtually unchanged from Friday's closings at around 10.0 percent in late trade.

Volatilities rose briefly early in the day as bonds dipped on news of a stronger-than-expected rise in February National Purchasing Management index. The index rose to 53.1 in February from 52.0 in January, against an average Wall Street estimate of 52.9.
"It (volatility) will probably come up a little more (prior to Greenspan testimony and jobs data)," said a brokerage trader at the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT).
But he added that there was little eagerness to bid up premiums in the pit.
"What probably will happen is premiums won't move very much and (bond) prices don't move very much," the trader said. "That implicitly is an increase in volatility."
Premiums should decline with time if implied volatility stayed steady because of theta, or time, decay.

He said he saw no big high-gamma bets often seen before important events or economic data. A high-gamma position, typically a result of buying short-dated options, gets quicker premium acceleration when the underlying market moves but are vulenerable to time decay.
"We'll probably see more of that tomorrow and after Wednesday," the trader said. "There's just so much time left before Friday."
But at the shorter end of the yield curve saw high-gamma options bid up.

Implied volatility for short-March Eurodollar options, which are options priced from March 1998 futures but expire in less than two weeks on March 14, rose significantly, while most conventional shorter dated options were narrowly mixed.
"That's not so surprising, considering that's the main high-gamma option for the week here," an investment bank trader said.
Short-March implied volatility gained some 1.5 point to 21.4 percent, while volatility for ordinary June and September options were up marginally at 10.5 and 14.1 percent.
Still traders said volume in short-March was not very big. Among the few large-lot trading today, one firm was seen buying 5,000 contracts of May 94.25/94.50 call spread.
